title: Fluid Mechanics: How Liquids and Gases Move
voiceNotes: Primary voice A (quantity and procedure). Voice B openers suit lesson 5 (the paper demonstration), lesson 11 (why golf balls have dimples) and lesson 12 (the equal transit time explanation), each of which starts from a puzzle.
description: Pressure, buoyancy, flow in pipes, pumps, drag, lift, open channels and model testing, worked on real dams, pipelines, golf balls and wings.
audience: Adults who have done Physics: Motion and Forces, know forces, moments and simple energy accounting from Engineering: Structures and Machines, and can use basic calculus ideas. They have not met pressure in fluids, Bernoulli's equation or the Reynolds number before. Thermodynamics and Energy Systems is a useful companion (it covers the steady-flow energy balance); this course uses only energy conservation from Physics I and does not repeat the steady-flow balance.
outcomes: You'll be able to work out the pressure at a depth and the force of still water on a dam wall or gate, and say where it acts.
You'll be able to tell whether a body floats and whether a floating hull will right itself.
You'll be able to use continuity, Bernoulli's equation and the momentum equation, and say which assumption fails when they do.
You'll be able to find a Reynolds number, judge laminar from turbulent flow and estimate head loss in a pipe system.
You'll be able to read a pump curve against a system curve and predict what speed changes, extra pumps and cavitation do.
You'll be able to explain drag, separation, lift and stall, including why golf balls have dimples.
You'll be able to classify open-channel flow, estimate speeds in channels and choose what to match when testing a model.

lessons.title: Pressure and depth
lessons.objective: Work out the pressure at a depth in a still liquid, say what fixes it (depth and density, not shape or volume), and read gauge and absolute pressure from a gauge or a manometer.

concepts.title: Density
concepts.summary: Mass per unit volume; the fluid property that sets how fast pressure grows with depth.

concepts.title: Hydrostatic pressure
concepts.summary: In a still liquid of uniform density the pressure rises by density times g times depth, the same in every direction.

concepts.title: Gauge and absolute pressure
concepts.summary: Absolute pressure is measured from a vacuum; gauge pressure is measured from the surrounding atmosphere.

concepts.title: Manometer
concepts.summary: A liquid column whose height difference balances a pressure difference.

concepts.title: Pascal's principle
concepts.summary: A pressure change in a confined liquid is passed on equally everywhere, so a larger piston gives a larger force over a smaller distance.

misconceptions: More water pushes harder. A deep pond has a higher bottom pressure than a wide shallow lake holding far more water, because pressure depends on depth only (Wikipedia, Liquid pressure).
Pressure depends on the container's shape, so a narrow standpipe and a lake behave differently. At the same depth the pressure is the same (DOE: a standpipe and a large lake).
Liquid pressure only pushes down. It acts equally in every direction and the net force on a surface is perpendicular to it.

A gauge that reads zero means there is no pressure. It means the pressure equals the atmosphere; the tyre on the car going up the mountain shows the gauge reading rise while the absolute pressure stays put.
A hydraulic jack gets something for nothing. The force multiplies by the area ratio and the distance divides by it.
sequence: Start with a diver's eardrums and a tank with holes at three heights: the deeper hole spurts faster.
Build the pressure from the weight of the column above: p = rho g h, so area cancels (DOE derivation).
Test it on cases: three vases of different shapes filled to the same depth, and a 3 m deep lake against a 6 m deep pond.
Gauge against absolute: add the atmosphere (101,325 Pa) to a gauge reading; the tyre going up a mountain.
The U-tube manometer: the liquid column balances the pressure difference, so the height difference is the reading; why mercury and why water.
Pascal's principle and the hydraulic press: 1 N in, 50 N out, and 100 cm of travel becomes 2 cm.
examples: Fresh water, take rho = 1000 kg/m3 and g = 9.81 m/s2. At 30 m deep the gauge pressure is 294 kPa and the absolute pressure is 396 kPa, about 3.9 atmospheres.
DOE: a tank 40 ft high filled with water of density 61.9 lbm/ft3 has 17.2 psi at the bottom; on a 20 ft diameter base that is a force of 7.78 x 10^5 lbf.
Wikipedia: for a 1.5 m wide section of dam, 3 m of water gives one quarter of the force of 6 m of water, while the average pressure is half.
A mercury manometer (13.534 g/cm3) with a 150 mm height difference shows a pressure difference of 19.9 kPa; the same height of water would show about 1.5 kPa.
A vacuum of 26 inHg gauge is 4 inHg absolute (30 minus 26).

lessons.title: Forces on dams and gates
lessons.objective: Find the total force of still water on a flat vertical wall or gate, say where it acts, and judge how it changes with depth.

concepts.title: Resultant hydrostatic force
concepts.summary: The total force on a submerged flat surface equals the pressure at its centroid times its area.

concepts.title: Centre of pressure
concepts.summary: The point where that force acts, always deeper than the centroid because pressure grows with depth; two thirds of the way down for a rectangle that reaches the surface.

concepts.title: Gravity dam
concepts.summary: A dam that holds back water by its own weight and the strength of its foundation.

concepts.title: Uplift
concepts.summary: Water pressure under a dam's base, which lifts it and has to be drained or allowed for.

misconceptions: The force on a dam depends on how much water is behind it. It depends on the depth and the wall's width (Wikipedia: pressure depends on depth, not volume held back).
The force acts at mid-depth. The pressure is larger low down, so the resultant acts lower: for a rectangle, d/3 above the base (LibreTexts, equation 8a).
Doubling the depth doubles the force. The force on a wall of fixed width goes with depth squared, so it quadruples.
A dam is designed for a horizontal push only. The foundation, the dam's weight and uplift all matter (Wikipedia, Gravity dam).
sequence: Pressure grows in a straight line with depth, so the load on a wall is a triangle: zero at the surface, rho g d at the base.
Total force = average pressure times area = pressure at the centroid times area (F = rho g yc A).
For a rectangle reaching the surface, F = (1/2) rho g B d squared: depth appears twice.
Where it acts: yp = Ix/(A yc); for the rectangle Ix = B d cubed over 3, so yp = 2d/3 below the surface, d/3 above the base.
A gate that does not reach the surface: use the depth of its centroid.
Warragamba: a gravity dam 142 m high, 8.5 m thick at the top and 104 m at the base; why the base is thicker than the top, and what the force calculation leaves out (uplift, foundation).
examples: A sluice gate 3 m wide holds back 2 m of water: F = 0.5 x 1000 x 9.81 x 3 x 2 squared = 58.9 kN, acting 0.67 m above the bottom.
A gate 2 m wide and 1.5 m high with its top edge 1 m below the surface: centroid depth 1.75 m, F = 1000 x 9.81 x 1.75 x 3 = 51.5 kN.
Warragamba Dam (gravity dam; deepest water 105 m): per metre of crest the water force is 0.5 x 1000 x 9.81 x 105 squared = 54.1 MN, acting 35 m above the base.
Raising the water from 4 m to 6 m multiplies the force by (6/4) squared = 2.25.

lessons.title: Floating and staying upright
lessons.objective: Decide whether and how deep a body floats from the weight of fluid it displaces, then use the metacentric height to judge whether a floating body will right itself.

concepts.title: Buoyant force
concepts.summary: The upward force on a body in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.

concepts.title: Principle of flotation
concepts.summary: A floating body displaces its own weight of fluid.

concepts.title: Metacentric height
concepts.summary: GM, the distance from the centre of gravity G up to the metacentre M; positive and large means a ship returns upright from a small heel.

concepts.title: Free surface effect
concepts.summary: Liquid sloshing in a partly filled tank shifts the centre of gravity toward the heel and reduces stability.

misconceptions: Heavy things sink. A steel ship floats because the hull and the air it encloses have an average density below the water's.
The buoyant force always equals the body's weight. Only for a floating body; a sunk body feels less buoyant force than its weight.
A floating body displaces its own volume of fluid. It displaces its own weight; the displaced volume equals its volume only when it is fully submerged (Wikipedia's note on this confusion).
A high centre of gravity always means a ship will tip. What counts is G against the metacentre M, and a large GM makes a ship stiff and uncomfortable, not safe in every way.
A tank that is full or empty is no safer than a half-full one. Only the partly filled tank has a free surface that shifts the weight.
sequence: Weigh a rock in air and in water: 10 N and 7 N, so the water pushed up with 3 N, the weight of the water it displaced.
Why iron sinks as a block and floats as a bowl: the same weight displaces more water.
Floating: weight equals buoyant force, so the fraction under water is the density ratio; sea water against river water.
Tipping: weight through G, buoyancy through B; when the hull heels B moves sideways; the metacentre M.
GM = KM minus KG; righting arm GZ = GM sin(heel) for small angles; low or negative GM, and the Vasa and the Herald of Free Enterprise as cases.
Free surface effect: grows with the cube of tank width; baffles into thirds cut it by 9.
examples: Rock: 10 N in air, 7 N hanging in water: buoyant force 3 N; density ratio to water 10/(10-3) = 3.3.
A 1-ton iron block displaces 1/8 ton of water; the same iron shaped as a bowl floats once it displaces 1 ton.
A hull of the same weight displaces 3.0% more volume in fresh water (998 kg/m3) than in sea water (1028 kg/m3), so it sits lower in a river.
With KM = 8.20 m and KG = 7.60 m (invented), GM = 0.60 m; at 10 degrees of heel the righting arm is 0.60 x sin 10 = 0.104 m.
A tank of width b has free surface effect proportional to b cubed. Split into thirds by two baffles it is 3 x (1/27) = 1/9 as large.

lessons.title: Flow rate and speed
lessons.objective: Use conservation of mass to find flow speeds and flow rates where a pipe changes size or branches, and say when density has to be carried through the calculation.

concepts.title: Volumetric and mass flow rate
concepts.summary: Volume per second is area times average speed; mass per second is density times that.

concepts.title: Steady flow
concepts.summary: Conditions at each point do not change with time, so nothing accumulates inside the control volume.

concepts.title: Continuity equation
concepts.summary: For steady flow the mass flow into a control volume equals the mass flow out; for constant density, Q in equals Q out.

concepts.title: When density can be held constant
concepts.summary: Liquids, and air below roughly 200 mph, can be treated as constant density.

misconceptions: Water flows faster in a wider pipe. For a fixed flow rate the speed falls as the area grows.
Speed goes with diameter. It goes with area, so with the square of the diameter (150 mm to 200 mm cuts the speed to 56%, not to 75%).
A narrowing 'chokes' the flow rate. In steady flow the rate is unchanged; the speed rises.
Mass flow and volume flow are the same thing. They are only proportional when density is constant, which fails for fast gas flows.
sequence: Define Q = A v and mass flow = rho A v, with the DOE pipe example (4 inch pipe at 14 ft/s).
Steady flow and control volume: what comes in must go out.
A pipe that widens (DOE: 22.4 ft/s to 12.6 ft/s from 6 to 8 inch) and one that narrows.
A branch: flows into the junction equal flows out (DOE Y-piece).
Real pipes: the Goldfields pipeline and a Snowy tunnel: speeds from design flows.
Where density must come along: compressible gas, and the 200 mph rule of thumb for air.
examples: A 150 mm main widens to 200 mm carrying 3.0 m/s in the narrow part: speed in the wide part = 3.0 x (150/200) squared = 1.69 m/s.
Goldfields pipeline: 23,000 kL/day = 0.266 m3/s through a 760 mm pipe (area 0.454 m2), so the average speed is 0.59 m/s.
Snowy Eucumbene-Tumut tunnel: capacity 113.2 m3/s, circular. If its diameter were 7.0 m (an assumption, the pack gives none) the speed would be 2.94 m/s.
A 0.40 m3/s main splits; one branch carries 0.15 m3/s and the other is a 0.20 m diameter pipe: speed in it = 0.25/0.0314 = 8.0 m/s.

lessons.title: Bernoulli's equation and when it fails
lessons.objective: Apply Bernoulli's equation between two points on a flow, and decide from the case whether its assumptions hold or a term is missing.

concepts.title: Bernoulli's equation
concepts.summary: Along a streamline in steady, incompressible, frictionless flow, pressure plus dynamic pressure plus rho g z stays constant.

concepts.title: Head
concepts.summary: Each term written as a height of fluid: pressure head, velocity head and elevation head add to the total head.

concepts.title: The assumptions
concepts.summary: Steady flow, constant density, negligible viscous friction, no pump or turbine between the points, and both points in one flow field.

concepts.title: Two uses
concepts.summary: Outflow speed from a tank, v = sqrt(2 g h), and flow measurement from a pressure drop across a venturi.

misconceptions: Faster-moving air always has lower pressure, anywhere. Bernoulli compares points along one flow; the air leaving a mouth has the same pressure as the room (Wikipedia: paper and ball demonstrations).
Bernoulli holds through any real pipe. It does not apply in the boundary layer, as in flow through a long pipe, and it cannot cross a pump (DOE).
Wings make lift because air has to travel farther over the top and arrives at the same time. There is no principle requiring equal transit time (Wikipedia; NASA).
Bernoulli's equation says pressure falls without limit as speed rises. It stops being valid before zero pressure; liquids cavitate.
sequence: From the energy view and from Newton's second law: the same equation, written three ways (pressure, head, energy per unit volume).
Use it on a contraction: speed from continuity, pressure change from Bernoulli.
A tank with a hole: Torricelli's v = sqrt(2 g h); real jets are a little slower (discharge coefficient).
A venturi meter: throat speed from the pressure difference; the factor of about 0.98 for friction (DOE).
The limits: friction, pumps and turbines, compressibility, unsteady flow, different flow fields.
Two bad explanations: the paper demonstration and the equal transit time wing; what is actually true.
examples: Water at 4 m/s enters a horizontal contraction with a quarter of the area: speed 16 m/s, pressure drop = 0.5 x 1000 x (16 squared - 4 squared) = 120 kPa.

lessons.title: Forces from jets and thrust
lessons.objective: Find the force of a jet on a plate or bucket and the thrust of an engine from the change of momentum of the fluid, and explain why the answers come out as they do.

concepts.title: Momentum equation
concepts.summary: The force on a fluid equals the rate at which its momentum changes; the fluid pushes back with an equal and opposite force.

concepts.title: Jet force on a deflector
concepts.summary: For a jet turned through an angle, the force along the jet is rho Q v times (1 - cos of the deflection).

concepts.title: Thrust
concepts.summary: Mass flow times the change in speed of the gas, plus a pressure term when the exit pressure differs from the surroundings.

concepts.title: Pelton wheel
concepts.summary: A turbine driven by jets; the force is largest when the wheel stands still and the power is largest when the wheel runs at half the jet speed.

misconceptions: A jet hitting a flat plate pushes with the force of its weight. The force is rho Q v, the momentum the plate removes each second.
A bucket that turns the jet back gives the same force as a flat plate. It gives twice as much, because the fluid's momentum is reversed.
An engine pushes against the air. Thrust is the reaction to accelerating a stream of gas; a rocket works in space because it carries its own oxidizer.
A turbine wheel gets the most power when it is held still. Held still it takes the most force and delivers no power; the best speed is half the jet's.
sequence: Newton's second law for a stream: force equals mass flow rate times change in velocity.
A jet on a flat plate: speed unchanged around the deflector, direction changed; F = rho Q v (LibreTexts).
Deflection angles: 90 degrees gives 1 x rho Q v, 120 degrees 1.5 x, 180 degrees 2 x.
The Pelton bucket: F = 2 rho Q (Vi - u); stationary wheel against moving wheel; best speed Vi/2.
Engines: F = mdot (ve - v0) (+ pressure term); two ways to get thrust: more flow or higher exit speed (turbofan against turbojet).
A broken pipe whips: DOE on pipe whip, the same reaction force.
examples: A 25 mm jet at 20 m/s: Q = 9.82 L/s, flat-plate force rho Q v = 196 N; hemispherical bucket 393 N; 120 degree deflector 295 N.
A turbojet passing 80 kg/s of air with exit speed 600 m/s at a flight speed of 250 m/s: thrust = 80 x (600 - 250) = 28,000 N (pressure term zero).
At 300 m/s flight speed the same engine (same flow, same exit speed) gives 80 x 300 = 24,000 N: thrust falls as the aircraft speeds up.
Pelton wheel, jet speed 60 m/s: force and power are largest at wheel speeds of 0 and 30 m/s respectively.

lessons.title: Laminar or turbulent: the Reynolds number
lessons.objective: Compute a Reynolds number for a pipe flow, decide whether the flow is laminar, transitional or turbulent, and say what that means for the velocity profile and for friction.

concepts.title: Viscosity
concepts.summary: A fluid's resistance to flowing past itself or a surface; liquids get thinner when heated, gases thicker.

concepts.title: Laminar and turbulent flow
concepts.summary: Smooth layers sliding over each other against irregular, mixing motion.

concepts.title: Reynolds number
concepts.summary: Density times speed times length over viscosity: the ratio of inertial to viscous forces.

concepts.title: Velocity profile
concepts.summary: Parabolic in laminar pipe flow, with a centre speed about twice the average; flat in turbulent flow.

misconceptions: Fast means turbulent. It is the Reynolds number that decides, which also depends on size and viscosity.
Viscosity matters only for thick fluids like honey. Water and air are viscous enough to set the regime in most pipes and around most bodies.
Heating thins every fluid. Liquids get less viscous when hotter, gases more viscous.
There is one sharp laminar-turbulent threshold. Sources put the transition anywhere from about 2000 to about 4000; the middle is unstable.
sequence: Dye in a pipe: a clear thread, a wandering thread, and a smeared cloud.
Viscosity: water 0.89 mPa s, air 18.5 micropascal seconds, and the University of Queensland pitch drop (230 billion times water).
The Reynolds number as the ratio of inertial to viscous forces; what the length is for a pipe.
Compute it for a few pipes; classify; the transition band and why sources differ.
Velocity profiles: parabolic against flat; centre speed about twice the average in laminar flow.
Why this will matter: friction behaves differently in the two regimes (next lesson).
examples: Water at 1.5 m/s in a 50 mm pipe (mu 0.89 mPa s, rho 1000): Re = 84270, turbulent.
Water at 0.05 m/s in a 20 mm tube: Re = 1124, laminar.
The speed at which a 20 mm tube of water reaches Re = 2000: 0.089 m/s.
DOE's 20 inch pipe at 5.35 ft/s with 200 F water: Re = 8.4 x 10^7, far into turbulence.
Laminar flow in a pipe with an average speed of 0.8 m/s has a centre speed of about 1.6 m/s.

figures.learnerAction: Raise the flow rate; the Reynolds number readout climbs and the dye thread changes.

figures.learnerAction: Toggle laminar and turbulent; read the centre speed in each.

distractorNotes.mistake: Reverses both trends.

questionPlan.answer: It is in the unstable band, so call it neither regime
choices: It is certainly laminar, because 3,000 is below 4,000
It is certainly turbulent, because 3,000 is above 2,000
It is in the unstable band, so call it neither regime
The sources disagree, so the Reynolds number is meaningless

distractorNotes.choice: It is certainly laminar, because 3,000 is below 4,000
distractorNotes.mistake: Ignores the transition band.

distractorNotes.choice: It is certainly turbulent, because 3,000 is above 2,000

distractorNotes.choice: The sources disagree, so the Reynolds number is meaningless
distractorNotes.mistake: They agree on the range; they differ on the exact edge.

lessons.title: Friction losses in a pipe
lessons.objective: Estimate the head lost to friction in a straight pipe with the Darcy-Weisbach equation, and predict how it changes with flow, diameter and regime.

concepts.title: Head loss
concepts.summary: The drop in total head along a pipe; the energy turned into heat by friction.

concepts.title: Darcy-Weisbach equation
concepts.summary: Head loss = f times (L/D) times v squared over 2g.

concepts.title: Friction factor
concepts.summary: 64/Re in laminar flow; in turbulent flow it depends on Re and relative roughness, read from the Moody chart.

concepts.title: Relative roughness
concepts.summary: Roughness height divided by pipe diameter.

misconceptions: Friction loss is proportional to speed. In turbulent flow it goes with speed squared; only in laminar flow does it go with speed.
A smoother pipe always helps. In laminar flow roughness does not matter at all.
A fatter pipe saves a little. At the same flow rate the head loss falls with the fifth power of the diameter, so doubling it cuts the loss 32 times.
The friction factor is a constant of the pipe. It changes with Reynolds number.
sequence: What head loss is and where the energy goes (it appears as heat).
Darcy-Weisbach: length, speed squared and diameter; a worked example with DOE's pipe.
The friction factor: laminar f = 64/Re; turbulent f from the Moody chart, between about 0.006 and 0.06.
Read the Moody chart: Re across, relative roughness as the curves.
Scaling: double the flow, double the diameter, laminar against turbulent.
Goldfields: why 400 m of climb needed 800 m of head.
examples: A 200 m pipe, 0.10 m diameter, water at 2.0 m/s, f = 0.02: head loss = 0.02 x (200/0.10) x (2.0 squared / (2 x 9.81)) = 8.2 m.
Double the flow: speed 4 m/s, loss x4 = 32.6 m (f unchanged).
Same flow in a 0.15 m pipe: loss falls by (0.10/0.15) to the fifth = 0.132 of the first value, about 1.07 m.
DOE: Re = 40,000 and relative roughness 0.01 read from the chart give f = 0.04; 100 ft of 20 inch pipe at f = 0.012 loses 0.32 ft.
Goldfields, with f = 0.02: head loss = 0.02 x (530,000/0.76) x (0.59 squared/(2 x 9.81)) = about 245 m, against a climb of nearly 400 m.

lessons.title: A whole piping system
lessons.objective: Add up the head a pump has to supply for a piping system from lift, friction and fittings, and judge when fittings, valves and sudden closures matter.

concepts.title: Extended Bernoulli equation
concepts.summary: Bernoulli's equation with a pump head added and a friction head subtracted.

concepts.title: Minor losses
concepts.summary: Head losses at bends, valves and fittings, each K times the velocity head, sometimes bigger than the friction in the pipe.

concepts.title: Equivalent length
concepts.summary: The straight pipe length that would give the same loss as a fitting.

concepts.title: Water hammer
concepts.summary: A pressure wave from suddenly stopping the flow; the spike is density times wave speed times the change in speed.

misconceptions: A pump only has to lift the water. It also has to pay the friction and fitting losses.
Minor losses are small. The name misleads; in a system with many fittings they can exceed the friction loss.
Closing a valve fast or slow makes no difference to the pipe. A fast closure sends a shock wave that can damage pipes and supports.
Head depends on the liquid. Head is a height, and the same height of any liquid corresponds to a different pressure.
sequence: Write Bernoulli between a reservoir surface and the outlet with pump head and friction head added (DOE, 67 ft).

Where fittings dominate: a short system with many valves; a half-closed valve.
Add up a system: static lift, friction, fittings.

lessons.title: Pumps and system curves
lessons.objective: Find where a pump and a pipe system settle by crossing the pump curve with the system curve, and predict what changes with speed, a second pump in series or in parallel, and cavitation.

concepts.title: Pump characteristic curve
concepts.summary: The head a centrifugal pump delivers at each flow rate at one speed; head falls as flow rises.

concepts.title: System curve
concepts.summary: Static head plus losses that grow with the square of the flow.

concepts.title: Operating point
concepts.summary: Where the two curves cross.

concepts.title: Pump laws
concepts.summary: Flow goes with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed.

concepts.title: NPSH and cavitation
concepts.summary: Net positive suction head is how far the pump's suction pressure is above the liquid's vapour pressure; below the pump's requirement, bubbles form and collapse and damage the impeller.

misconceptions: A pump delivers a fixed flow. The flow depends on the system it works against.
Two identical pumps in parallel double the flow. They give less than twice, because the higher flow raises the system's head loss (DOE).
Doubling pump speed doubles the power. It multiplies power by eight.
Cavitation is just noise. It erodes and vibrates the impeller.
sequence: Pump curve: head against flow at constant speed.
System curve: static head plus a parabola of friction.
The crossing is the operating point; open a valve and the system curve flattens.
Speed changes with the pump laws: DOE's 1800 to 3600 rpm example.
Series add head at the same flow; parallel add flow at the same head; which suits what.
Hydraulic power rho g H Q and efficiency.
Cavitation and NPSH; the Goldfields and Snowy cases.

lessons.title: Drag and the boundary layer
lessons.objective: Use the drag equation and the idea of a boundary layer to say how drag changes with speed and shape, and why a dimpled golf ball travels farther than a smooth one.

concepts.title: Drag equation
concepts.summary: Drag = one half rho v squared times a drag coefficient times a reference area.

concepts.title: Boundary layer
concepts.summary: The thin layer next to a surface where the speed goes from zero to the free stream value.

concepts.title: Flow separation
concepts.summary: The boundary layer lifts off, leaving a wide low-pressure wake and high form drag.

concepts.title: Form drag and skin friction
concepts.summary: Pressure drag from the shape, and viscous drag along the surface.

concepts.title: Drag crisis
concepts.summary: A sphere's drag coefficient falls sharply near a Reynolds number of 300,000 when its boundary layer turns turbulent.

misconceptions: A rough ball must have more drag than a smooth one. In a certain range of Reynolds numbers it has less, because the rough surface trips the boundary layer into turbulence, which stays attached longer.
Doubling speed doubles the drag. Drag goes with speed squared, the power needed with speed cubed.
Streamlining means a pointed front. The rear shape matters most: tapering the downstream side cuts drag.
A turbulent boundary layer always means more drag. It resists separation better and can give a narrower wake.
sequence: A moving body: the boundary layer, from zero speed at the surface to the stream speed.
Drag equation; Cd collects the shape and flow effects; typical values.
Squared and cubed: the car at 50 and 100 mph.
Bluff against streamlined; form drag against skin friction.
Separation: slowing flow, rising pressure, boundary layer stalls; the wake.
The sphere: Cd against Reynolds number, drag crisis, and the golf ball.
examples: Typical Cd (NASA): flat plate 1.28, wedge with the wedge downstream 1.14, sphere 0.07 to 0.5, bullet 0.295, airfoil 0.045; the flat plate has about 28 times the airfoil's drag at the same area.
Car at 50 mph needs about 10 hp to overcome drag; at 100 mph, 80 hp.
Drag on a car body: 0.5 x 1.2 x 25 squared x 0.3 x 2.2 = 248 N (air 1.2 kg/m3 supplied).
NASA: a baseball at 100 mph has Re = 2.2 x 10^5 and Cd of about 0.5 smooth, about 0.3 with stitches.
Golf: about 300 to 500 dimples; a dimpled ball flies farther at the same speed because the boundary layer turns turbulent and separates later.

lessons.title: Lift and stall
lessons.objective: Use the lift equation to scale lift with speed, judge explanations of lift for what is false and what is right, and say why a wing stalls.

concepts.title: Lift
concepts.summary: The part of the fluid force perpendicular to the oncoming flow; it needs the flow to be turned.

concepts.title: Lift equation
concepts.summary: Lift = one half rho v squared times a lift coefficient times wing area.

concepts.title: Angle of attack and stall
concepts.summary: Lift rises with angle until the upper-surface flow separates; beyond that angle lift falls.

concepts.title: Pressure and momentum views
concepts.summary: Pressure differences and the turning of the flow are two views of the same force.

misconceptions: The air going over the top must meet the air going under at the rear edge. No principle requires equal transit time; the top air is much faster than that would need.
Bernoulli and Newton compete. Both are correct and describe the same force.
A wing stalls when it is going too slowly. Stall is a flow condition at a large angle of attack, though a slow wing needs a larger angle.
Only wings make lift. Any body that turns the flow net does, including a car body and a golf ball with backspin.
sequence: Lift is the force perpendicular to the flow; the wing turns the air down.
Why the common explanations fail (equal transit, half a venturi).
Pressure difference and flow turning: both are right (NASA).
The lift equation and scaling with speed.
Angle of attack: lift rises, then the upper surface flow separates and the wing stalls.
Wright brothers' wind tunnel; spoilers on race cars; golf ball backspin.
examples: A wing lifts 6,000 N at 50 m/s; at 70 m/s: 6,000 x (70/50) squared = 11760 N.
A 20% heavier aircraft needs lift 20% greater at the same angle and area: speed x sqrt(1.2): 50 m/s becomes 54.8 m/s.
The Wrights' 1901 glider gave about 1/3 of the lift predicted from Lilienthal's data, so they built their own wind tunnel.
NASCAR roof spoilers 'kill lift' in a spin.

lessons.title: Open channels and the Froude number
lessons.objective: Classify open-channel flow with the Froude number, predict where a hydraulic jump forms, estimate channel speed with the Manning formula and see how flow over a weir depends on head.

concepts.title: Free surface flow
concepts.summary: Gravity, not an imposed pressure, drives the flow, and the depth is part of the answer.

concepts.title: Froude number
concepts.summary: Speed over the speed of shallow waves, U over sqrt(g d); below 1 subcritical, above 1 supercritical.

concepts.title: Hydraulic jump
concepts.summary: An abrupt rise in depth with loss of speed where fast flow meets slow, dissipating energy.

concepts.title: Manning formula
concepts.summary: Average speed = (1/n) x hydraulic radius to the 2/3 x slope to the 1/2.

concepts.title: Weir
concepts.summary: A barrier whose flow depends on the head over it: Q goes with H to the 3/2 for a rectangle, 5/2 for a V-notch.

misconceptions: Open-channel flow is driven by pressure like pipe flow. It is dominated by gravity and has a free surface.
Fast water must be deep water. Supercritical flow is fast and shallow; a hydraulic jump turns it to slow and deep.
A hydraulic jump creates energy. It dissipates it, which is why spillways are built to make one.
Manning's n is a precise property. It is an estimate; direct measurement is better.
sequence: What differs from a pipe: the free surface and gravity.
The Froude number: wave speed and what subcritical and supercritical mean.
A hydraulic jump: fast and shallow to slow and deep; needs supercritical flow upstream; used in stilling basins.
Manning's formula and the hydraulic radius; roughness coefficient.
Weirs: the head and the flow.
A Snowy or Warragamba spillway case to read.
examples: A channel 2.0 m deep with speed 3.0 m/s: Fr = 3.0/sqrt(9.81 x 2.0) = 0.68, subcritical.
At the toe of a spillway the flow is 0.5 m deep at 12 m/s: Fr = 5.4, supercritical, so a jump will form where the downstream water is deep enough.
A rectangular weir with the head up from 0.20 m to 0.30 m passes 1.84 times the flow; a V-notch 2.76 times.

lessons.title: Models and dimensionless numbers
lessons.objective: Choose which dimensionless number a model test must match, scale a model result to full size, and say when a test cannot be trusted.

concepts.title: Dimensionless group
concepts.summary: A combination of variables with no units, such as Reynolds, Froude or Mach number.

concepts.title: Buckingham pi theorem
concepts.summary: n variables with k fundamental dimensions can be reduced to n - k dimensionless groups.

concepts.title: Similitude
concepts.summary: A model with the same shape, similar flow pattern and the same force ratios as the full-size case.

concepts.title: Partial similarity
concepts.summary: Often only the most important number can be matched, and the rest is judged.

misconceptions: A model should be tested at the real speed. To match the Reynolds number a smaller model may need a faster flow.
Match every number. Usually not possible; engineers choose the one that governs and judge the rest.
A coefficient measured at one condition holds anywhere. Not across Mach number or Reynolds number ranges.
Similarity only needs the same shape. It needs the same force ratios.
sequence: Why test models: the Wright brothers and the wind tunnel; William Froude's towed ships.

Matching Froude number: free surface models (ships, spillways).
When the test cannot be matched: the NASA warning on drag coefficients at the wrong Mach number.

Same fluid at 1/40 scale with the same Reynolds number: model speed 40 times as great.
A 1:25 spillway model matches Froude number: prototype 10 m/s gives model speed 2.0 m/s.
Pipe pressure drop depends on 7 variables (drop, density, viscosity, speed, diameter, length, roughness) and 3 fundamental dimensions, so 4 groups.
